summary: Rand's view of what standards computer service centers on the network should follow, written as input for a panel discussion at the October 1971 meeting. It argues that common appearance and behavior across service centers would help users, and that service centers must follow the official network protocols.

eli5.summary: If every shop of a kind looked and worked the same, customers would find them easy. This note argues that computer service centers should follow common rules so users can move between them.

subtitle: Making network services easy to use by following common rules.

tldr.problem: Different ARPANET service centers have inconsistent access procedures, accounting methods, job submission formats and documentation, making it hard for users to move between services.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 231 proposes standardizing how service centers handle login, remote job entry, accounting, scheduling, and documentation so users need only one method to access many services.
tldr.outcome: Common standards enable users to dynamically choose the best service center for each job based on cost and turnaround time.

today: RFC 231 is a seminal argument for standardization in network services. It anticipates by decades the modern understanding that API consistency and user experience standardization drive network adoption and utility.

sections.title: Why Service Centers Need Standards
sections.content:
RFC 231 argues that the ARPANET community needs standards for how service centers present themselves to remote users. The document states that it is assumed service centers will conform to official network protocols—this is essential since their practices affect the wider network and are crucial to the effectiveness of minimal hosts like Terminal IMPs.

Standardization benefits two important groups: the ultimate user community (researchers and their support staff) and those responsible for implementing resource access programs. Without standards, each service center requires different learning and different code to access.
sections.eli5: Shops that follow the same rules are easier to use. People can work at different shops without retraining, and computer programs can connect to many shops with the same code.

sections.title: Areas Needing Standardization
sections.content:
RFC 231 identifies several key areas for standardization. Remote Job Entry (RJE) is immediate: two different RJE facilities on the network use different protocols. Login procedures across all systems ask for the same information (password, identification, account number) but in different formats. Charging algorithms use the same ingredients (storage, I/O, connect time, CPU) but calculate them differently, making cost comparison impossible.

Job scheduling, priorities and status information could enable a useful query service: a user could ask which Tenex machine would complete a job fastest and cheapest. Other areas include off-line services (graphics, tape facilities), documentation formats, operating schedules, and procedures for system failures.
sections.eli5: When you want to submit a job, every service asks for your password and account number but in different ways. When you want to know how much it costs, they calculate using different rules. One standard way for each would make everything simpler.

sections.title: Standards Implementation
sections.content:
RFC 231 suggests that either the Resource Notebook should be expanded into a service center standards notebook, or a separate item should be created for that purpose. Some items should be standardized in format rather than the services themselves—for example, operating schedules vary by time zone and storage capabilities differ, but they can all be documented consistently.

The document argues that service centers intending to attract a significant network user community should adopt psychology appropriate to market-oriented service provision. Network personnel tend to have a different approach to computing than that required by a service bureau, and standardization would help bridge this gap.
sections.eli5: There should be a handbook describing what each service center promises and how to use it, so users know what to expect everywhere.
